item.title: The New ADHD Medications, Explained for Patients
item.description:
ADHD

The New ADHD Medications, Explained for Patients

Four new options for ADHD treatment have arrived. Most patients still shouldn’t switch.

Posted September 25, 2026

Key points
  • Simtriyo, approved in July 2026, spares dopamine and disrupts sleep less, but its benefit is smaller.
  • Qelbree starts working faster than Strattera; generic Vyvanse may matter more than any new drug.
  • If your current medication works, new options ask nothing of you. If it doesn’t, start by asking why.

Three ADHD medications have reached American patients in the past five years, and a fourth was approved this July. For a field that spent two decades cycling the same molecules through new delivery systems, that is a genuinely unusual stretch. It has also produced a wave of questions in my office, most of which reduce to one: Should I switch?

For most patients the answer is No, and understanding why requires knowing what each new option actually is.

Simtriyo (centanafadine) is the newest, approved by the FDA in July 2026 for ages six and up. It works mainly on norepinephrine, one of the two brain chemicals the older stimulants act on, while largely leaving dopamine alone. That design has a purpose: Dopamine is where the euphoria and abuse potential of amphetamines comes from, so a medication that sidesteps it may carry less of both. The trade-off shows up in the trial data. In placebo-controlled studies, centanafadine’s benefit was roughly a third to half the size of what amphetamines produce. Its clearest advantage was sleep: Patients reported substantially less insomnia than is typical for stimulants. My reading of the evidence is that Simtriyo will earn a real place for patients whose anxiety, sleep, or substance-use history makes amphetamines a poor fit, and that patients doing well on their current stimulant have little reason to trade a larger effect for a smaller one. (I’ve published a detailed comparison of the trial numbers for readers who want them.)

Qelbree (viloxazine) arrived in 2021 for children and 2022 for adults. It’s a cousin of an older non-stimulant, Strattera, with two practical differences: It tends to start working in one to two weeks rather than four to eight, and it avoids a genetic quirk that makes Strattera unpredictable in a minority of patients. It also interacts with caffeine — a detail worth knowing for a teenager who lives on energy drinks. Like Strattera, it carries a warning about suicidal thoughts in young people, which in practice means closer check-ins during the first weeks — the same vigilance we apply to antidepressants.

Generic Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine) may matter to more patients than either new molecule. Since the brand lost exclusivity, multiple manufacturers have entered, and for patients paying cash the price difference is substantial. The supply has been uneven, however — some strengths fill easily while others disappear for weeks — but the direction is toward a first-line stimulant becoming affordable.

The remaining recent arrivals are new packages for old molecules: Jornay PM, a methylphenidate taken at night so it’s working when a child wakes; Azstarys, a partial-prodrug stimulant; and Onyda XR, a liquid form of clonidine for children who can’t swallow pills. Each solves a specific practical problem. None changes what the medication does once it’s in the bloodstream.

Here is the comparison I find myself drawing in clinic: Choosing an ADHD medication is like choosing a route to work. The amphetamines are the highway — they're the fastest, the most direct, and the standard against which everything is judged, although with real hazards that require attention. The non-stimulants are surface streets; slower, gentler, and sometimes exactly right — because of a history of addiction, an anxiety disorder that stimulants inflame, or side effects that never settled.

New roads are worth celebrating. Most commutes still belong on the highway.

Two more cautions as these medications get marketed: First, “new” and “better” are different claims, and for every medication above, the placebo-controlled effect sizes remain publicly available for anyone to check. Second, no head-to-head trial compares Simtriyo with the stimulants; the comparisons in circulation are statistical reconstructions, mostly funded by manufacturers, and should be read with that understanding.

If your current medication is working — attention improved, side effects tolerable, mornings functional — the arrival of new options is interesting news that requires nothing of you.

If your current medication isn’t working, this is the richest moment in 20 years to revisit the question with your prescriber, and the right conversation starts with why the current one is failing: too little benefit, too much side effect, or a schedule that doesn’t fit your life. Each answer may point to a different medication on this longer list.

item.title: It’s Not All on You: The Urge to Carry Too Much
item.description:
Stress

It’s Not All on You: The Urge to Carry Too Much

How we learn to carry more than our share.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Over-responsibility can create accountability for things we cannot fully control.
  • The expectations we inherit can reinforce the pressure to handle things alone.
  • Letting go of some responsibility doesn’t mean abandoning what is ours to own.

Sometimes I find myself working late into the night. I may or may not be writing this post far beyond when I was supposed to be wrapping up work. And full confession: I’m not sure why I do this. I’m a therapist in private practice—there is no deadline I’m trying to meet, no supervisor I’m trying to impress, no promotion I’m vying for. And yet, somewhere within me there is a sense of urgency that says, “Not enough. Do more. You need to accomplish more today."

“You need to accomplish more today.” When I hear that inner voice get loud in myself or in clients, I find that I start to spiral with questions: Who says I need to accomplish more? What is more? What counts as an accomplishment? And those are all important questions, but for the purpose of this post, I want to focus on the operative word spoken by that inner voice: “you.” It never says “we need to accomplish more.” It’s always on my shoulders.

Tracing the Roots

There’s a name for some of this: over-responsibility. It’s the idea that we take ownership of things that are outside of our control—the thoughts and feelings of others, outcomes that we cannot determine, events in the past that we cannot alter. For many of us, this can be a powerful way to feel more in control of our lives. But as a social worker, I’m equally interested in the external systems that reinforce this.

Not all pressure comes from the inside. Some we inherit. I see within me multiple intersecting sources of this story. Being raised male in this world taught me to provide and fix, to be strong and not need support. Living in America foisted a rugged individualism on me that I just can’t seem to shake. I’ve never been a fan of Westerns and yet some part of me feels like I’m a solitary lawman responsible for taming the Wild West. My Judaism came with a heaping helping of generational persecution. I inherited the lineage of a people who were exiled and persecuted across much of Europe for centuries, and in that inheritance I also hold the story that if I don’t make myself important I am expendable. Even my work as a therapist brings with it a moral imperative to heal others… or else!

The common thread in all of these narratives is that it’s all on me. How lonely. How untrue. And yet, how real it feels to many of us. How often that current is what keeps us up late finishing the essay.

Laying Down the Burden

How often do you take it all onto your shoulders? For many of the folks I work with, even hearing this called out brings up some powerful defenses. “Are you trying to tell me I shouldn’t be responsible for my actions?” or “I like the fact that I set goals and crush them. I don’t want to lose that." And I get that. But when faced with this line of reasoning, my next question is, “How often do you feel like everyone is letting you down and if they would just get their you-know-what together everything in your life would be fine?” That one is usually met with less resistance. The truth is that these two patterns often share real estate—either it’s all my responsibility or none of it is my responsibility. Either it’s mine to fix or I’m taking my toys and going home. The more challenging middle path is taking responsibility for our part without making ourselves responsible for the whole thing.

I had a falling out with a friend recently. Well, more of a cooling off, actually. We were so close for so many years but it became clear that things had changed. At first, I searched for something I could do to fix this. Surely if things changed then I could change them back. And then when that didn’t work, I found myself getting angry. If they just made more of an effort to understand me then this wouldn’t be an issue! See that? All my responsibility. Not my responsibility. But the truth of the matter was infinitely more complex. It’s probably true that we both made choices that inadvertently hurt the other, not because we didn’t care about each other but because what each of us needed pulled us in opposite directions.

But that perspective is only possible when we allow ourselves to put some of the burden down. Sometimes putting down a burden means giving it to someone or something. I gave mine to the Merced River. No joke. We were traveling in Yosemite with some friends and I was breathing deeper than I had in months. It was the end of a long day lounging by the river, and I found myself floating on my back staring up at Wawona Dome. I felt myself give my weight to the water and I felt the water hold me up. I closed my eyes and just floated. I must have had a stupid grin on my face, because my friend asked me what I was thinking about. I said, “Nothing,” and asked why he asked. He said I looked peaceful, and it looked good on me.

The river didn’t solve my problems. It didn’t absolve me of my responsibilities. But for a moment, it let me put the burden down. It held me up for a change.

Rivers are pretty low stakes, though. They don’t ask anything of us. It’s much harder for most of us to let another person do what the water did—a friend with whom you share how you really feel, a partner who takes the kids so you can rest. Letting ourselves be held by another person asks us to acknowledge something our inner solitary lawman would rather ignore: We were never meant to do this alone.

The river reminded me that it wasn’t all on me. It never could be. And it’s not all on you, either.
